<reason>Both sides were competent and disciplined, but PRO held the moderate motion more securely than CON dismantled it. CON's two live routes were (1) unadministrability/enforcement failure and (2) borrowed consent for children. On (1), PRO's answer — that adopting the standard normatively includes reviewability and that "you cannot fix weak review by abolishing the permission" — blunted the attack, and the contract-law analogy (we void coerced contracts rather than ban contracts) was a clean weighing move. On (2), PRO's counter that children cannot consent to anything yet we routinely act through parents (boarding school, piano training, vegetarianism) exposed that CON offered no principled reason dress is the sole exception; CON's A1 answer ("yes" to uniforms, "no" once the norm is religious) looked evasive, and PRO exploited it in closing. CON's redundancy argument ("redundant where safe, unpoliced where dangerous") was PRO's toughest pressure, but PRO's response — easy cases validate a standard, contested cases are where the conditions do sorting work — plus the motion's ceiling function against assimilationist overreach gave PRO a live answer. CON's entanglement point (courts probing apostasy costs) went largely unanswered, but PRO's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a real execution cost that partially explains that gap. Overall, PRO made the decisive clash (does a conditional permission beat abolition?) easier to decide and answered more of the incoming pressure squarely.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's rebuttal sequence on parental choice: forcing CON to answer whether religious schools may ever set dress expectations for children with real alternatives, then showing in Rebuttal 2 and Closing that CON's "uniforms yes, religious norms no" position rests on a consent principle that would outlaw ordinary parental decisions across a child's entire life — a contradiction CON never resolved.</best_rebuttal>
